content: Manroot, also known as Wild Cucumbers (genus Marah), are flowering plants belonging to the gourd family, Cucurbitaceae. These plants are native to western North America and are sometimes referred to by the common name Old man in the ground. Characteristics Manroots are perennial plants that grow from large, tuberous roots. Their stems are typically stout and either rough or hairy, equipped with coiling tendrils that allow them to climb other plants or spread rapidly across flat ground. The leaves of these plants are often lobed, with some species having leaves with up to seven lobes. The fruits of manroots are particularly distinctive, being large and either spherical, oval, or cylindrical in shape. They range in size from a minimum of 3 cm in diameter to as long as 20 cm, and many species have fruits covered in long spines. The shape of the leaves and fruits can vary significantly, not only between individual plants but also on the same vine. The name manroot and the anthropomorphic nickname old man are derived from the appearance of the tuber, which often has swollen lobes and arm-like extensions when unearthed. In older plants, the tuber can grow to several meters in length and weigh over 100 kg. The genus name Marah is derived from a Hebrew word meaning bitter, reflecting the bitter taste of all parts of these plants. Distribution With the exception of Marah gilensis, which is found in a limited range in west-central Arizona, all other species of manroot inhabit overlapping ranges that extend from southern Canada to northern Mexico. While the Coastal Manroot (Marah oreganus) extends inland into Idaho, most other species, excluding M. gilensis, are confined to regions bordering the Pacific Ocean. Taxonomy Species within the genus Marah are known to hybridize freely where their ranges overlap. This, combined with the variability in leaf and fruit morphology within and between species, makes precise identification of specimens challenging. Some taxonomists include manroots in the genus Echinocystis. When considered a separate genus, Marah includes six or seven species, some of which have well-defined varieties. Medicinal Uses Marah oreganus was used by Native American tribes for various medicinal purposes. The Chinook people prepared a poultice from the gourd, while the Squaxin tribe mashed the upper stalk in water to soak aching hands. The Chehalis tribe burned the root and mixed the resulting powder with bear grease to treat scrofula sores. The Coast Salish people made a decoction to address venereal diseases, kidney problems, and scrofula sores. Seeds of Marah fabaceus have been reported to have hallucinogenic properties. The tubers of M. fabaceus and M. macrocarpus contain saponins, which can act as a natural soap but are toxic if ingested. Like many medicinal plants, some species of Marah are toxic, and deaths have been reported from their ingestion.
